::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The end-of-course project goal

Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python,
with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
**By the end of the course**, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

-   well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
-   a pipeline automated with GNU Make
-   a reproducible Quarto report
-   a Docker container for the computational environment
-   a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing
:::

## Milestone 4 summary

This milestone ties your project together: **one command runs the whole analysis**,
your code is tested, your report reads like a finished paper,
and you fix what reviewers pointed out.

- [ ] Write a `Makefile` so `make all` runs every script, renders the report and publishes it
- [ ] Move some code into functions (**at least one per team member**) and write tests for them
- [ ] Polish your report: no visible code, numbered and cross-referenced figures and tables, citations
- [ ] Address feedback from the TAs and from the peer review

::: callout-important
## See what a finished Milestone 4 looks like

An example Milestone 4 that corresponds to our expectations is here:
**[Breast Cancer Predictor 3.0.0](https://github.com/ttimbers/breast-cancer-predictor/tree/3.0.0)**.
Look at its `Makefile`, `src/` and `tests/` folders.
It uses conda for its environment: ignore that part and keep the uv/renv setup from Milestone 2.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Readings for this milestone

-   [Data analysis pipelines with GNU Make](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/pipelines-make.html) and the [Makefile cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/makefile.qmd)
-   [Testing](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/testing.html), then [pytest](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/testing-python-pytest.html) (Python) or [testthat](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/testing-r-testthat.html) (R)
-   [Reproducible reports with Quarto](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/reproducible-reports-quarto.html) and the [Quarto cheatsheet](../cheatsheets/quarto.qmd) (you practised these in Individual Assignment 3)
:::

### 1. Write a `Makefile` that runs everything

Put a file named `Makefile` in the root of your repository, as you did in Individual Assignment 4.
It needs:

-   an `all` [target]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="In a Makefile, a target is a named thing Make can build: usually a file (like a figure), or a name for a group of steps (like all or clean). You run one with make followed by its name, e.g. make all."}: runs the whole analysis from top to bottom, including `publish`
-   a `clean` target: deletes everything the pipeline made, so `make all` can start fresh
-   a `publish` target: copies the rendered report to `docs/index.html`,
    replacing the steps you did by hand in [Milestone 2](milestone2.qmd#publish-your-report-on-github-pages)
-   **real file targets** for the other steps, with their dependencies (the data **and** the script),
    so Make only reruns what changed.
    Only `all`, `clean`, `publish` and similar group names may be [phony]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A phony target is a name for a group of steps, not a file Make creates. You list it under .PHONY so Make always runs it, even if a file with that name exists. In this milestone, all, clean and publish can be phony; the other targets must be real files."}.
-   comments that explain each rule, and a `README` section that says how to run it

Your scripts run in the container, so the commands in the rules start with `uv run` (Python),
for example `uv run python scripts/download_data.py ...` and `uv run quarto render ...`.
Run the pipeline with `docker compose run --rm analysis-env make all`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Example: the `publish` target

Change the report's path to your own:

```{.makefile filename="Makefile"}
publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: reports/<your-report>.html
	mkdir -p docs
	cp reports/<your-report>.html docs/index.html
	touch docs/.nojekyll
```

Because `docs/index.html` depends on your rendered report, `make publish` copies it only when the report has changed.
Commit and push `docs/` after it runs.
:::

### 2. Write functions and test them

Look for code that repeats (cleaning several columns the same way, many similar plots, tuning several models)
or that you would reuse in another project.

1.  **Write at least one function per team member**, following the textbook's
    [workflow for writing functions and tests](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/testing.html#workflow-for-writing-functions-and-tests-for-data-science):
    write the documentation first, then the tests, then the function body.
2.  **Put them in their own files:** `src/*.py` (Python) or `R/*.R` (R).
    One function per file, or all in one file, both are fine.
3.  **Use them in your scripts** with `import` (Python) or `source()` (R).
4.  **Write tests in `tests/`** with [`pytest`](https://docs.pytest.org/) (Python)
    or [`testthat`](https://testthat.r-lib.org/) (R).
    Add the test package to your environment, and say in your `README` how to run the tests in the container.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How your functions are marked

-   **Quality:** each function does one thing, and returns a value unless it is meant to write a file or plot.
-   **Usability and readability:** clear names and arguments; [black](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html) (Python) or [tidyverse](https://style.tidyverse.org/) (R) style.
-   **Documentation:** a docstring (Python) or roxygen comment (R) saying what it does, its arguments and what it returns.
-   **Tests:** they cover expected cases, edge cases and errors.

More functions than the minimum are welcome, but each one is held to these standards.
:::

### 3. Polish your report

A reader who is not a data scientist should not be able to tell that code made the report.
Render it to HTML (that is the version on GitHub Pages); a PDF as well is optional.

- [ ] A table of contents
- [ ] Citations from a BibTeX file, with a reference list at the end
- [ ] Figures with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them, at a sensible size
- [ ] Tables with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them
- [ ] The text refers to figures and tables with cross-references (`@fig-...`, `@tbl-...`), never typed numbers
- [ ] Values in the text (accuracy, sample size...) come from inline code, not typed in by hand
- [ ] No code shows in the rendered report, only its output

### 4. Address feedback

#### From the TAs

Fix what the TAs pointed out in earlier milestones.
Then submit a regrade request on Gradescope for that question,
with **links to the pull requests or commits** that show the change.
If the TA confirms the fix, you get back **50% of the points you lost** on that question.
Keep the request easy to follow, or we can't give points back.

#### From the peer review

Address **at least one peer review item per team member** (a team of 4 fixes at least 4).
List them in a `CHANGELOG.md` in the root of your repository:
for each item, the feedback, what you changed, and a link to the evidence (an issue, pull request, commit or lines of code).
Feedback that the TAs also gave can go in too.
See [keepachangelog.com](https://keepachangelog.com/) for an example.

### 5. Update your `README`

Your `README` must take someone **from a fresh clone to the rendered report**:
pull the image, run `make all` in the container, and how to run the tests.
Also say how to run `make clean`.

::: callout-important
## 5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions

If someone can't run your whole pipeline by following your instructions
**exactly as written**, you lose all 5 points.
Test them on **both Windows and Mac**.
If your team doesn't have both, ask another team to test them.
:::

## Submission instructions

1.  Just before you submit, create a GitHub release named exactly `3.0.0`
    ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
2.  On Gradescope, enter these three URLs (there is no PDF to make):
    -   the GitHub release
    -   your group project's repository (general one without GitHub release)
    -   your report on GitHub Pages

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself before submitting

- [ ] From a fresh clone, `make all` in the container runs everything and updates `docs/index.html`
- [ ] Running `make all` a second time does nothing; `make clean` removes everything the pipeline made
- [ ] At least one tested function per team member, in `src/` or `R/`, used by your scripts
- [ ] All tests pass in the container
- [ ] The rendered report shows no code and every item in the polish list above is done
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` lists at least one peer review item per team member, with links
- [ ] Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your `README` steps exactly
- [ ] Your report on GitHub Pages matches your release
- [ ] You created the `3.0.0` release
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Teamwork expectations (these are marked)

-   **Everyone contributes equally** to code, writing and project management,
    shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
-   Use the [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow):
    a branch for each feature or fix, reviewed by at least one teammate before the pull request is merged.
-   Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages
    (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
-   Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack.
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don't have to be complicated.
-   Your analysis should be correct and run reproducibly from your `README` instructions.
-   Follow the [black style guide](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html) (Python)
    or the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/) (R).
-   Don't commit generated files, except `docs/`, which GitHub Pages needs.
-   Write your `README` in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.
:::
